note: Per-country resource entries shown in the record popup, grouped into collapsible categories with a count each. Every entry is a record with its own description and source link, tagged by lens, so they can be toggled and indexed like anything else on the map. Written per country because the answer differs per country; the guides carry the explanation, these carry the resources. Categories marked scope=release are only shown on release and biosafety-decision records and in the country box, because a consultation window is about a decision being made — on a clinic or a company record it is noise. The rest are shown everywhere, because testing, complaining and certification apply whatever the reader is looking at.

categories.label: WHO CERTIFIES, AND WHAT A POSITIVE TEST COSTS
LEGAL HELP, IN THIS FIELD SPECIFICALLY

test.d: Lateral flow strips, the same format as a pregnancy test. Crush tissue or seed in water, dip, read in five to ten minutes. Sold to anyone, a few pounds each, in packs. Strips are trait-specific, so know which trait to look for before buying.
Strips plus the extraction kits that go with them, sold internationally — which matters because the trait to test for differs by region.
Sells in small quantities with published prices, which makes it the most usable of the three for someone testing a handful of samples rather than a lorry.

decides.d: Every party to the Cartagena Protocol must name a contact for biosafety, and the list is public. For most of the world it is the only named biosafety contact that exists, and it holds the decisions filed for that country.

notice.d: Parties file their decisions here, and for most first imports for release a public consultation is required beforehand. For countries with no notice venue of their own, this is the only place an application becomes visible in advance.

certify.d: The global umbrella for organic standards, which exclude engineered material by definition in every member scheme. Use it to find the certifier operating where you are: a positive test costs an operator the certification and the price premium immediately, without a hearing.

legal.n: Center for Food Safety — legal programme
legal.d: Has brought most of the significant US litigation in this field, including the cases that vacated approvals for engineered alfalfa and sugar beet pending fuller environmental review. Takes information from the public and publishes model ordinance text for local measures.

Files formal objections to EU approvals and requests internal review of Commission decisions — a specific legal mechanism most people do not know exists. Its published objections are the template for anyone drafting one.

Environmental lawyers who litigate on process rather than on the technology: whether an assessment was adequate, whether a consultation was real, whether access to documents was refused lawfully. That is the ground on which these cases are usually won.

legal.n: Public Patent Foundation — OSGATA v. Monsanto
legal.d: Brought the case in which organic and conventional growers sought protection from patent claims over seed that arrived on their land without them planting it. The court declined jurisdiction on the strength of a binding commitment not to sue over trace presence, which is now the operative assurance.

open.d: US notices with a comment window, searchable and subscribable by email. Thirty to sixty days, and a comment filed inside it must be addressed in the decision. Subscribe rather than check: thirty days is short if you hear on day twenty-eight.

Every European assessment is published in full with the panel's reasoning and opened for comment, typically for thirty days. The document states what was assessed, which makes it possible to comment on what was not.

Australia publishes each application, the risk assessment plan and the proposed field sites, then invites comment for around thirty days. Knowing the sites before the decision is what makes a local objection possible.

decides.d: Authorises releases and publishes the permit and notification files daily, searchable by state, crop and organism. It gives the states a release is authorised in and never the coordinates.
A plant engineered to make its own insecticide is regulated as a pesticide, not as a crop. Registration documents state what the grower is obliged to do around it, which the release permit does not.

complain.d: The state employs the inspectors, can enter a field and issues the penalties. Sending an account to Washington first is the commonest reason it goes nowhere. Quote the permit number.
Drift reports go first to the state lead agency, which inspects and can fine; the EPA holds the national record. Report while residue is still detectable.
A worker exposed while applying or working around these chemicals can file, anonymously if they choose, and retaliation for filing is separately unlawful.

notice.n: Regulations.gov — file a comment, read the response
notice.d: Where a US comment is submitted and where every other comment on the docket can be read, including the agency's published response to them.

certify.d: Search any certified operation and find its certifier. Certifiers must investigate complaints about operations they certify, and can suspend certification without a court or a regulator.

test.d: Most states run an official seed testing laboratory. Charges are modest, and an enforcement body is likelier to act on a result from a laboratory it already recognises.

decides.d: Decides releases on advice from ACRE, and holds the public register of applications and consents.

complain.d: Holds notifications for every laboratory in Britain working with engineered organisms and investigates complaints about containment — one of very few places where contained use is reportable by the public at all.

Report a dead animal, pet or bee colony you believe was poisoned by pesticide and the state collects the carcass and pays for the analysis. Results are published and feed into whether an approval is kept.

certify.d: Certifies organic production in the UK, and organic standards exclude engineered material outright. A positive test costs the grower the certification and the price premium with it.

decides.d: Authorises plants with novel traits and publishes a decision document for each. Canada is one of very few registers listing edited and inserted-gene products side by side, which makes it the best place to check what an organism actually is.
Assesses anything sold as food and publishes the decisions.

complain.d: Hold pesticide applicator licensing and take drift complaints. As in the US, the province inspects and the federal body sets the rules.
Takes reports about permitted activities and publishes enforcement outcomes.

certify.d: Organic standards exclude engineered material; the CFIA lists accredited certifiers, and a positive test costs the operator the certification.

decides.d: Runs the release register and publishes trial locations — in Germany down to the land parcel, which is more than most countries give.

complain.d: The states inspect and enforce; the federal office authorises. A complaint goes to the Land, not to Berlin.

certify.d: Certifies that livestock were fed without engineered feed — the part of the supply chain consumer labelling law does not touch, and where most of the volume is.
The largest German organic association; its standard excludes engineered material outright.

decides.d: Authorises releases; trial locations are published under the EU deliberate release directive.
Assesses risk and publishes its opinions.

complain.d: The regional service inspects and takes drift complaints.

certify.d: Holds the register of certified operators and the list of certifying bodies.

decides.d: Authorises on advice from the Comisión Nacional de Bioseguridad. Spain grows more engineered maize than the rest of the EU combined, so this is the one member state where cultivation is the live question.

complain.d: Aragón and Catalonia hold most of the area; the community inspects, not Madrid.

certify.d: One of the largest organic certifiers in Spain.

decides.n: Office of the Gene Technology Regulator
decides.d: Licenses every dealing with an engineered organism, and publishes the licence, the risk assessment and the approved field sites — which few regulators do before a decision.

complain.d: The state, not the federal agency, employs the inspectors who can enter a field and issue penalties. Find yours before writing anything.
Inspects licensed sites and publishes monitoring reports.

certify.d: Certifies to a standard excluding engineered material.

decides.d: Decides releases under the environment ministry and publishes its meeting minutes, which is where an approval first becomes visible.

complain.d: Have authority over releases in their state and are closer than Delhi.

certify.d: The national organic programme and its accredited certifiers.

decides.d: Issues the technical opinion that authorises a release, and publishes approvals.

complain.d: Handle environmental damage locally, and are usually quicker to inspect than the federal body.

notice.d: Where approvals and hearings are announced.

certify.d: Holds the register of certifying bodies.

decides.d: Advises on releases and publishes its advice.
The ministry authorises.

complain.d: Inspects and takes complaints on food and plant safety.

certify.d: The Dutch organic certifier; tell them if certified land is affected.

decides.d: Authorises releases.
Handles cultivation and coexistence.

complain.d: Also administers the compensation fund that pays a grower whose crop loses its non-GM or organic status because of a neighbour, financed by a levy on engineered cultivation. Very few countries have one.

decides.d: Authorises agricultural releases.
Shares responsibility for environmental release.

notice.d: Japan's national node; approvals and decisions are published here.

certify.d: The Japanese organic standard and its registered certifiers.

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs
decides.d: Issues biosafety certificates and publishes lists of approved events. China approved its first domestic maize and soy for planting in 2023 after more than a decade in which food-crop approvals were effectively frozen, so the list is worth checking rather than assumed.

complain.d: Handle enforcement, and are the level at which unapproved planting has actually been acted on — several provinces have destroyed unauthorised maize.

certify.d: The national organic standard excludes engineered material; certification is issued through accredited bodies under CNCA.

decides.d: Authorises on advice from the interministerial commission. Italy has used the EU cultivation opt-out, so the live questions here concern imports and feed rather than fields.

complain.d: The regions inspect and take drift complaints.

certify.d: One of the larger Italian certifiers, operating internationally.

decides.d: Authorises releases. National law prohibits the cultivation of engineered crops, so a release here would be a contained or research matter rather than a field.

complain.n: PIORiN — plant health and seed inspection
complain.d: Inspects seed and plant health, and is the body that would act on unauthorised planting.

certify.d: One of the Polish organic certifiers.

decides.d: Authorises releases of engineered plants and publishes the applications.

complain.d: The county board inspects locally and takes complaints.

certify.d: The Swedish organic standard, stricter than the EU organic baseline and dominant in Swedish retail.

decides.d: Authorises releases. Austria invoked the safeguard clause against an EU-approved variety and defended it for years — that fight is why the EU cultivation opt-out exists at all.

complain.d: The states inspect, and several have declared themselves GM-free through regional law and grower agreements.

certify.d: The largest Austrian certifier; the organic share of farmland here is among the highest in Europe, which is itself a coexistence constraint.

decides.d: Authorises releases. Switzerland has extended its moratorium on growing engineered crops repeatedly since 2005 while continuing to import engineered feed and to host some of the largest agricultural biotechnology companies in the world.

complain.d: The canton inspects and enforces; the federal office authorises.

certify.d: The Swiss organic label; its standard excludes engineered material and it covers most Swiss organic production.

decides.d: Authorises under the Gene Technology Act, which is unusual in requiring an applicant to show benefit to the community and sustainability, not only safety.

complain.d: Inspects food, feed and aquaculture, and takes reports.

decides.d: Decides applications under the HSNO Act and publishes them with a public submission period. New Zealand has permitted almost no outdoor release, so most of the register is contained laboratory work.

complain.d: Handles biosecurity and unauthorised organisms, including material arriving in imported seed.

certify.d: The main New Zealand organic certifier.

decides.n: Department of Agriculture — GMO Act registrar
decides.d: Authorises releases under the GMO Act. South Africa is the only country in Africa where engineered maize is a staple eaten directly rather than fed to animals, which makes the food-crop question live rather than hypothetical here.

certify.n: SAOSO — South African Organic Sector Organisation

decides.d: The advisory commission that wrote Resolution 173/2015, which decided an edited organism carrying no foreign DNA is not a GMO and needs no biosafety approval. Chile, Brazil, Colombia, Paraguay and Honduras all adopted versions of it — more countries follow this text than any other on the subject.

complain.d: The food and agricultural health service; inspects and enforces.

certify.d: Argentine organic certifiers, mostly serving the export market.

decides.d: Handle permits and the inter-secretarial biosafety commission. Mexico sits inside the centre of origin for maize, where wild relatives and thousands of local varieties still grow, and has restricted engineered maize on that basis.

complain.d: The federal environmental protection agency; takes citizen complaints about environmental damage and is obliged to respond.

certify.d: A Mexican organic certifier working with smallholder and indigenous producers.

decides.d: Authorises releases and publishes decisions. Kenya lifted its ban on engineered crop imports in 2022 while a court challenge to that decision was still running, so the position has been contested rather than settled.

complain.d: Inspects seed and plant health and is the body that acts on unauthorised material.

certify.d: East African organic mark and its certifiers.

decides.d: The federal biosafety portal, which publishes applications, advice and the register. Authority is split between the federal level and the three regions, which is why a Belgian answer usually has two halves.

complain.d: The regions inspect and enforce; the federal level authorises.

certify.d: One of the main Belgian organic certifiers.

decides.d: Licenses both contained use and deliberate release, and publishes the register — unusual in combining the two in one agency.

complain.n: Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine
complain.d: Inspects and enforces on seed and crops.

decides.n: DGAV — Direcção-Geral de Alimentação e Veterinária
decides.d: Authorises and holds the cultivation register. Portugal is one of only two EU states with commercial engineered maize, so its coexistence rules are among the few actually in use.

complain.d: Portuguese coexistence rules require a grower to notify neighbours before planting, and to keep isolation distances. That notification is the document to ask for.

decides.n: Ministry of Rural Development and Food
decides.d: Authorises. Greece has used the EU cultivation opt-out, so the questions here concern imports and feed.

complain.d: The region inspects and enforces; the ministry authorises.

decides.d: Authorises releases and keeps the register.

complain.n: ÚKZÚZ — Central Institute for Supervising and Testing in Agriculture
complain.d: Inspects seed and crops and runs the official testing laboratories.

decides.d: Authorises. Hungary's constitution commits the country to agriculture free of engineered organisms, which is unusual — most prohibitions sit in statute rather than in a constitution.

complain.n: NÉBIH — National Food Chain Safety Office
complain.d: Inspects and enforces, including seed testing for engineered content.

decides.d: Authorises releases.

complain.d: The food safety authority; inspects and takes complaints.

decides.d: A standing board rather than a ministry department, which publishes its decisions and minutes.

complain.d: Inspects food, feed and seed, and runs the official testing.

decides.d: Authorises. National law prohibits the cultivation of engineered crops outright.

certify.d: A Bulgarian organic certifier working across the region.

decides.d: Authorises. Most Croatian counties have declared themselves GM-free, which was done by county decision rather than national law.
Russia prohibits the cultivation and import of engineered crops for planting, with an exception for research. The register therefore records feed and food approvals rather than releases.

complain.d: Handles food safety and consumer complaints.

certify.d: The national organic standard and its register of certified producers.

decides.d: Authorises. Ukraine's registration system has long lagged actual planting, which is documented rather than alleged — surveys have repeatedly found unregistered engineered soy in the field.

complain.n: State Service on Food Safety and Consumer Protection
complain.d: Inspects and enforces on food, feed and seed.

decides.d: Authorises releases and publishes decisions. Nigeria approved Bt cowpea in 2019 — the first engineered food crop released in sub-Saharan Africa, and one of very few anywhere developed by a public institute for a staple its own country eats.

complain.d: Food and drug control; takes complaints on labelling and food safety.

certify.d: Holds the participatory guarantee scheme used by most Nigerian organic producers.

decides.d: Authorises releases and runs the public consultation. Ghana approved Bt cowpea after Nigeria, following the same public-institute route.

complain.n: Plant Protection and Regulatory Services Directorate

decides.d: Authorises under the biosafety proclamation, which was substantially relaxed in 2015 after being one of the strictest in Africa.

certify.d: Certification is mostly for export coffee and sesame.

decides.d: Handles applications. Egypt is the largest wheat importer in the world, and its state tender specifications on engineered content set terms for exporters across several continents — a buyer decision that functions as regulation.

complain.n: Ministry of Agriculture — Central Administration for Plant Quarantine
complain.d: Inspects imports and enforces at the border.

decides.d: Authorises. Bangladesh released Bt brinjal in 2013 — the first engineered food crop grown by smallholders in South Asia, and the most studied case of one.

complain.d: The extension service is the practical contact for a grower.

decides.d: Handles approvals. Pakistan grows engineered cotton at scale, much of it from seed that entered the country before any approval — adoption preceding registration, as in Paraguay.

complain.d: Seed inspection and enforcement is provincial.

decides.d: Advises the ministries that authorise releases and food use.
Issues the release decision.

certify.d: Accredited under the national organic standard.

decides.n: Department of Agriculture — Bureau of Plant Industry
decides.d: Authorises releases. In 2024 the Court of Appeals revoked the approvals for Golden Rice and Bt eggplant through a constitutional environmental remedy citizens can invoke directly — the only case anywhere of a court withdrawing a granted biosafety approval at the public's request.

complain.n: Bureau of Plant Industry — regional offices

certify.n: OCCP — Organic Certification Center of the Philippines

decides.n: Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment
decides.d: Authorises environmental release; the agriculture ministry handles cultivation. Vietnam approved engineered maize in 2014 and grows a modest area while importing several million tonnes of engineered maize and soy each year for feed.
Handles applications. Thailand permits field trials but has not authorised commercial cultivation, while remaining a large exporter of rice and a major feed importer.
Handles agricultural approvals; the food ministry handles food use. Korea is one of the largest importers of engineered maize and soy in the world and grows none commercially.

complain.n: MFDS — Ministry of Food and Drug Safety
complain.d: Handles food labelling complaints, which is where most Korean disputes arise.

certify.d: Under the national environment-friendly agriculture scheme.

decides.d: Authorises under the Biosafety Law. Turkey prohibits cultivation of engineered crops entirely while approving specific events for animal feed — one of the clearest splits between what may be grown and what may be imported.

certify.d: Accredited under the national organic regulation.

decides.d: Authorises. Chile permits engineered seed to be grown only for export multiplication, not for domestic planting — so a field of it here is producing seed for somebody else's country, which is a distinction most registers do not make.

certify.d: Accredited under the national organic law, largely for export fruit and wine.

decides.d: Authorises releases and publishes the resolutions. Colombia adopted a version of Argentina's Resolution 173, so edited organisms with no foreign DNA fall outside biosafety approval here.

The seed and plant health authority. Engineered soy arrived in Paraguay across the border and was widely planted before it was legal, so this office's task became regularising a situation rather than deciding one — adoption first, approval afterwards.

certify.d: Small, mostly export sesame and sugar.

decides.d: Authorises through an inter-ministerial cabinet rather than a single agency. Uruguay is unusual in maintaining a national coexistence and traceability system for engineered and non-engineered maize.

complain.n: MGAP — Ministerio de Ganadería, Agricultura y Pesca

decides.d: Bolivia permits one engineered soy event and no others, while its constitution restricts engineered organisms — a narrow legal opening inside a broad prohibition.

complain.d: Food and agricultural health service; inspects and enforces.

certify.d: The Bolivian organic producers' association, which runs participatory certification.

decides.d: Peru has a moratorium on the entry and release of engineered organisms, extended to 2035 — the longest in force anywhere, and grounded in protecting the country's crop diversity rather than in a safety finding.

certify.d: Largely for coffee, cacao and quinoa export.

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture — National Committee for Transgenic Plants
decides.d: Authorises field trials. Israel permits research and trials but no commercial cultivation, while hosting a substantial plant biotechnology sector — and it approved cultivated meat earliest of anywhere.
Handles food and feed approvals and labelling. Saudi Arabia imports nearly all its grain, so the questions here are about what arrives rather than what is grown.

complain.d: Takes food safety and labelling complaints.

certify.d: Under the national organic agriculture programme.

decides.n: Ministry of Climate Change and Environment
decides.d: Handles biosafety and food import approvals. The Emirati Genome Programme sequences the whole national population with the data held by the state, which is the more consequential genetic question here.
Authorises under the Biosafety Act and publishes applications with a public comment period — which is more than most of the region provides.

certify.d: Certifies halal status for food sold to around two billion people, and its rulings cover enzymes, gelatine and cultured products made with engineered organisms — a question no food regulator answers and this one must.

decides.d: Assesses novel foods, and was the first authority anywhere to approve cultivated meat for sale, in 2020. A city-state importing most of its food has reasons a farming country does not.

complain.d: Advises on release and contained use.

decides.d: Approves food use and requires labelling. Taiwan permits no commercial cultivation of engineered crops and prohibits them in school meals, which is an unusual and specific restriction.

certify.d: Under the national organic agriculture act.

decides.n: National Council for Science and Technology
decides.d: Approves confined field trials. Uganda has run trials for years — banana, cassava, maize — without a biosafety law in force, because successive bills were passed by parliament and not signed. Research proceeds; commercialisation cannot.

certify.d: The Ugandan organic movement, which runs certification for the export market.

decides.d: Authorises. Tanzania halted its trials in 2018 and ordered material destroyed, having previously operated a strict liability rule that made researchers personally liable for any damage — which is why almost nobody applied.

complain.n: Tanzania Plant Health and Pesticides Authority

decides.d: Authorises. Zambia refused engineered maize as food aid during the 2002 famine, which remains the most cited instance of a country declining it under emergency conditions and is still the reference point in African debate.

certify.n: Organic Producers and Processors Association of Zambia

decides.d: Authorises and runs the testing laboratory. Zimbabwe requires imported grain to be milled before distribution so it cannot be planted, which is a practical answer to the food-aid question Zambia answered by refusal.

Authorises. Burkina Faso grew Bt cotton at scale and then withdrew it in 2016 because the fibre was shorter and worth less — the only case of a country abandoning a commercial engineered crop for quality reasons rather than safety or politics. Target Malaria's gene-drive mosquito work continues here.
Authorises. Sudan grows Bt cotton commercially, one of the few African countries doing so.

certify.d: Mostly gum arabic and sesame for export.

decides.d: Handles approvals. Morocco has no commercial engineered cultivation and is a substantial exporter of fruit and vegetables to the EU, which shapes what it permits.

complain.d: The food safety office; inspects and enforces.

certify.d: Under the national organic law, largely export-facing.

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Development
decides.d: Algeria prohibits the import and cultivation of engineered seed outright, one of the more absolute positions in the region.

certify.d: Small and mostly for dates and olive oil.

decides.d: Handles approvals. Tunisia has no commercial cultivation; imported feed is the practical question.

complain.n: Direction Générale de la Santé Végétale

certify.n: CTAB — Centre Technique de l’Agriculture Biologique

decides.d: Serbia prohibits the cultivation and trade of engineered crops under its GMO law, which has been a live issue in its EU accession talks because the prohibition is stricter than EU law permits.
Authorises and runs the national biosafety clearing-house node, which is more complete than most in the region.

decides.n: Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources
decides.d: Handles biosafety. Kazakhstan has a BSL4 laboratory and a substantial biological research sector, so containment rather than cultivation is the live question here.

certify.d: Under the organic production law, largely for grain export.

decides.n: Ministrstvo za naravne vire in prostor
decides.d: Authorises. Slovenia has no commercial cultivation and much of the country is covered by regional GM-free agreements made between growers rather than by national prohibition.

complain.d: Food safety administration; inspects and enforces.

certify.d: Accredited under the national organic scheme.

decides.d: Authorises releases and holds the register.

complain.d: The central control and testing institute; inspects seed and crops.

decides.d: Authorises releases.

complain.d: The state plant service; inspects seed.

decides.d: Authorises releases.
Handles the cultivation register; most Latvian municipalities have declared themselves GM-free.
Authorises releases.
Holds the cultivation register and the coexistence rules.
Authorises. Luxembourg has declared itself GM-free in practice and hosts Eurofins, the largest food testing network in the world, which runs much of Europe's commercial GMO detection.

complain.n: Administration des services techniques de l’agriculture

decides.d: Authorises. Iceland has permitted contained barley production for pharmaceutical proteins — molecular farming in greenhouses rather than fields, which is the form this takes where outdoor release is impractical.

complain.n: MAST — Icelandic Food and Veterinary Authority

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture, Rural Development and Environment
decides.d: Authorises. Cyprus requires labelling of GM food at retail more strictly than the EU baseline, including in restaurants.
Authorises releases.

complain.n: Malta Competition and Consumer Affairs Authority

decides.d: Authorises. Costa Rica permits engineered crops to be grown for seed export while not authorising them for domestic cultivation — so it hosts the production of a crop its own farmers may not plant. Several cantons have declared themselves GM-free.
Authorises. Cuba develops its own engineered crops through state institutes rather than importing them, which is a route no other country in the region takes.

certify.d: Largely state-run and domestic rather than export-certified.

decides.d: Venezuela's seed law prohibits engineered seed outright and was written with substantial public participation — one of the few seed laws anywhere drafted that way.

complain.d: The agricultural health institute; inspects and enforces.

decides.n: National Biosafety Focal Point — Ministry of Environment
decides.d: Handles biosafety. Sri Lanka attempted a nationwide switch to organic farming in 2021 by banning agrochemical imports outright; the resulting yield collapse and reversal is the most cited case anywhere of what happens when input systems change without transition.

certify.d: Largely for tea and spice export.

decides.d: Handles biosafety. Nepal prohibits the import of engineered seed, and the practical question here is what crosses the open border with India rather than what is authorised.

complain.n: Plant Quarantine and Pesticide Management Centre

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock and Irrigation
decides.d: Handles approvals. Myanmar grows engineered cotton, much of it from seed that arrived without formal approval — the same adoption-before-registration pattern seen in Pakistan and Paraguay.
Handles biosafety under the Cartagena Protocol; there is no commercial cultivation.

certify.d: Participatory schemes for rice and pepper.

decides.n: Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment
decides.d: Handles biosafety; no commercial cultivation is authorised.
Handles biosafety. Papua New Guinea holds extraordinary crop and forest diversity and very little regulatory capacity, which is the combination the Cartagena Protocol was written for.

complain.n: National Agriculture Quarantine and Inspection Authority

certify.d: Mostly coffee and cocoa for export.

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture — Biosecurity Authority of Fiji
decides.d: Handles biosafety and biosecurity together, which is common across the Pacific: island states treat an engineered organism as an import question first.

certify.d: A regional standard used across the Pacific islands.

decides.d: Handles biosafety.
Handles seed and crop approvals.
Handles biosafety under the Cartagena Protocol.
Authorises. Panama grows engineered maize on a modest scale and its position matters disproportionately because of what transits the canal.
Ecuador's constitution declares the country free of engineered seed and crops — one of only a handful of constitutions anywhere addressing this directly, alongside Hungary's.

complain.d: The agricultural quality agency; inspects and enforces.

certify.d: Largely for banana, cacao and coffee export.

decides.d: Handles approvals. Guatemala sits inside the centre of origin for maize, where wild relatives and thousands of local varieties still grow, so gene flow here is a different question from gene flow in a field in Iowa.
Authorises. Honduras was the first Central American country to permit engineered maize commercially, and adopted a version of Argentina's Resolution 173 on edited organisms.

decides.n: Ministry of Environment — National Biosafety Committee
decides.d: Handles approvals. Cameroon's agricultural research institute holds germplasm collections for crops grown across central Africa that exist nowhere else, which is what benefit-sharing arrangements are written about.

Handles approvals. Côte d’Ivoire has a BSL4 laboratory under construction — one of only three high-containment facilities in Africa — while scoring among the lowest on biorisk governance of any country with one.
Handles approvals under the biosafety law. Senegal signed the Nagoya–Kuala Lumpur liability protocol but has not ratified it, which is the commonest position in the region.

complain.n: Direction de la Protection des Végétaux

decides.d: Handles approvals. Mali is a party to the Nagoya–Kuala Lumpur liability protocol, unlike most of its neighbours, so damage from a release has an agreed remedy framework here.
Handles biosafety. Mozambique has run confined trials of drought-tolerant maize and its regulations were revised in 2014 to permit them.
Authorises. Malawi approved Bt cotton for commercial planting in 2018, one of the few African countries to do so, and is a party to the Nagoya–Kuala Lumpur liability protocol.
Authorises under the Biosafety Act. Namibia requires labelling of GM food and its rules are among the more developed in southern Africa outside South Africa.

decides.n: Department of Waste Management and Pollution Control
decides.d: Handles biosafety. Botswana imports most of its grain from South Africa, so what arrives is the practical question rather than what is grown.
Handles biosafety. Rwanda has run confined trials of engineered potato and cassava through its agricultural research board.
Handles biosafety. Jordan imports nearly all its grain, and its labelling requirements are the practical point for a consumer.

complain.d: Handles food labelling and safety complaints.

decides.d: Handles biosafety. Lebanon has no biosafety law in force and imports most of its food, which makes the labelling and import questions the only live ones.

certify.d: Small, largely for olive oil and wine.

decides.n: Ministry of Environmental Protection and Agriculture
decides.d: Handles biosafety. Georgia sits inside a centre of origin for wheat and grape, holding hundreds of endemic varieties, which is the reason its position matters beyond its size.

certify.d: Elkana and the biological farming association.

decides.d: Handles biosafety; no commercial cultivation is authorised.

decides.n: Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources
decides.d: Handles biosafety.
Handles biosafety. Moldova is a party to the Nagoya–Kuala Lumpur liability protocol, which most of its neighbours are not.
Handles biosafety. Albania prohibits the cultivation of engineered crops and is a party to the liability protocol.

decides.n: Council of Ministers — Food Safety Agency
decides.d: Handles biosafety, split across the entities, which makes a single national answer difficult.

decides.n: Ministry of Agriculture, Natural Resources and Rural Development
decides.d: In 2010, after the earthquake, Monsanto offered several hundred tonnes of hybrid seed as a donation and Haitian peasant organisations publicly burned it, arguing it would displace local varieties and create dependency on purchased seed. It remains the most direct rejection of donated seed anywhere, and it was made by farmers rather than by a government.

complain.d: Plant protection; inspects imports and seed.

decides.n: Bhutan Agriculture and Food Regulatory Authority
decides.d: Bhutan has a national policy of moving to fully organic agriculture, which excludes engineered material by definition rather than by biosafety decision — the only country to have set that as a national goal.

Handles biosafety. Gabon hosts one of only three high-containment BSL4 laboratories in Africa, at the Franceville medical research centre, while scoring among the lowest of any country with one on biorisk governance.

decides.n: Ministère de l’Environnement (Democratic Republic of the Congo)
decides.d: Handles biosafety and is a party to the Nagoya–Kuala Lumpur liability protocol. The country holds the second largest tropical forest on Earth and very little regulatory capacity, which is the combination the Protocol was written for.
Handles biosafety. Angola formerly refused engineered food aid unless milled, following Zimbabwe's approach rather than Zambia's outright refusal.

decides.n: Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development
decides.d: Handles biosafety. Madagascar's endemic biodiversity is among the highest on Earth and largely found nowhere else, which makes any deliberate release a different order of question here.

decides.d: Handles biosafety. Benin operated a formal moratorium on engineered crops for a decade, one of the few African states to legislate a time-limited prohibition rather than simply not deciding.

decides.d: Handles biosafety. Nicaragua permits no commercial cultivation and its seed law protects farmer varieties, which is the position most of Central America has moved away from.

subnational._note: Matched on the location string of whatever the reader has open, so a record in Iowa shows Iowa's inspector rather than the national one. This is the level that employs the people who can enter a field, and almost every national entry on this map points down to it without naming it.

_generic.d: Employs the inspectors, can enter a field and issues the penalties. Find yours in the directory; sending a report to Washington first is the commonest reason it goes nowhere.

Iowa.n: Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship
Iowa.d: Pesticide Bureau takes drift complaints and inspects. Iowa plants more engineered maize and soy than any other state, so this is the busiest such office in the country.

Illinois.d: Bureau of Environmental Programs handles pesticide misuse complaints and licensing.

Nebraska.d: Pesticide programme takes drift reports and inspects applicators.

Minnesota.d: Runs an incident response programme for pesticide drift and spills, and publishes its enforcement actions.

Indiana.d: Unusually, Indiana's pesticide regulator sits at Purdue rather than in a department, and it publishes case outcomes.

Kansas.d: Pesticide and fertilizer programme takes complaints and inspects.

Missouri.d: Bureau of Pesticide Control. Missouri was the centre of the dicamba drift complaints, which ran to thousands of reports in a single season.

Arkansas.d: The board that restricted dicamba use after a season of drift complaints, and the clearest case of a state body acting against a federally registered product.

California.d: Runs its own registration regime alongside the federal one and publishes a full pesticide use report — the most detailed public record of what is sprayed anywhere in the United States.

Texas.d: Handles pesticide complaints and applicator licensing.

North Dakota.d: Pesticide programme; North Dakota grows most of the US canola and a large share of the soy.

South Dakota.n: South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources

Wisconsin.n: Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection
Wisconsin.d: Agricultural resource management division takes drift complaints.

Michigan.n: Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development
Michigan.d: Pesticide and plant pest management division.

Oregon.d: Handles pesticide complaints, and holds the record of the creeping bentgrass escape — engineered grass found outside its trial site and still being managed two decades later.

Washington.d: Pesticide management division takes drift complaints.

Hawaii.d: Hawaii hosts most US seed-corn winter nurseries, so more engineered field trials happen here per acre than anywhere else in the country, and county-level restrictions have repeatedly been litigated.

Puerto Rico.d: Puerto Rico is the other major winter nursery site for seed corn, and is a US territory rather than a state, so federal rules apply with no state legislature above the department.

_generic.d: The federal office authorises; the Land inspects and enforces. A complaint goes to the Land, not to Berlin.

Bavaria.n: Bayerisches Landesamt für Gesundheit und Lebensmittelsicherheit
Bavaria.d: Bavaria declared itself GM-free and was the state where the Bablok honey case arose.

Baden-Württemberg.d: The regional councils inspect and enforce.

Lower Saxony.d: Lower Saxony holds much of Germany's arable land and its seed industry.

Saxony-Anhalt.d: Saxony-Anhalt was where most German engineered maize trials took place before cultivation ended.

_generic.d: The community inspects and enforces, not Madrid.

Aragón.n: Departamento de Agricultura, Ganadería y Medio Ambiente de Aragón
Aragón.d: Aragón plants more engineered maize than any other region in the European Union.

Catalonia.n: Departament d’Acció Climàtica, Alimentació i Agenda Rural
Catalonia.d: Catalonia is the second largest area of engineered maize in the EU.

Andalucía.n: Consejería de Agricultura, Pesca, Agua y Desarrollo Rural
Andalucía.d: Andalucía holds the largest organic area in Spain, which makes coexistence the live question here.

_generic.d: State committees have authority over releases in their state under the 1989 rules, and are closer than Delhi. Several states have refused trials the GEAC approved.

Maharashtra.d: Maharashtra grows the largest area of Bt cotton in India and has seen unapproved herbicide-tolerant cotton planted at scale.

Telangana.d: Much of India's cotton seed production happens here, so seed rather than crop is the question.

Kerala.d: Kerala declared itself an organic state and has refused engineered crop trials outright.
